newsitem.title: INDIA: Major India market-boosting steps seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Major India market-boosting steps seen unlikely.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda is unlikely to announce any major initiatives in measures he has promised to unveil later this week to bolster capital markets, analysts said on Tuesday.

"We are not expecting any major announcements," said an official of Jardine Fleming Broking India. He said major initiatives affecting company tax regulations were unlikely without prior discussion in the federal parliament.
"I don't expect them to announce any revenue-negative measures ahead of the budget," said an analyst at an Indian brokerage. The federal budget is due on February 28.
Deve Gowda said on Monday that some economic policy measures would be announced this week, but said parliament's approval will be needed for further measures.
"Some decisions will be coming in the next two to three days," Deve Gowda told a business gathering at the All India Association of Industries in Bombay.

There has been widespread speculation that the government may repeal a controversial minimum alternate tax (MAT) imposed in the 1996/97 (April-March) budget which took away tax breaks given to companies making large capital investments.
Bankers to some of India's leading private companies described MAT as a disincentive to building new capacities.
"This dampener came at a time when global commodity prices were falling and India was reducing its customs duties," said a top official of a term-lending bank.
"There are lot of myths about MAT," said Kiran Nanda, economist at cement firm Gujarat Ambuja Cements.
"People ask why companies shouldn't be paying tax -- the answer is you need incentives for large infrastructure projects."
The government is unlikely to abolish double taxation on company dividends -- which the media thinks it would do -- because of its revenue implications, analysts said.
"Such steps are unlikely when the government is coping with a budget deficit at 5.2 percent of GDP," said an analyst.

A Bombay broker said one positive step the government could announce right away, without hurting revenues, would be to raise a 20 percent ceiling on foreign institutional investment in the State Bank of India (SBI) to 24 percent, bringing it on par with other firms.
SBI is India's largest commercial bank and a market favourite.
Some market players said the prime minister's attitude was more important than any concrete measures he might announce.
"The government wants to boost investor confidence," said B.K. Taparia, executive director of the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI), the leading long-term lender.
"The signals are positive -- whatever the government does now will be keenly watched," Taparia said.
The research head of an Indian broking firm said the government had been promising measures to "kickstart the markets" since December, when stock markets had fallen sharply.
"Now there is no longer any need for a kickstart," he said.

The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index has risen by over 15 percent in the New Year. Most analysts feel the current revival, though largely speculator-driven, is based on India allocations by major foreign funds, and would be sustained.
